podcast.body: Released in 1991, this album continued the band's commercial success, also selling a million copies in Canada. It marked a significant delve into Canadiana, with Gord Downie drawing deep inspiration from Canadian places, people, and locations. The original working title for the album was "Saskadelpia," but it was ultimately released under the more rural Canadian term "Road Apples," referring to horse manure. "Road apples in 1991. It also sold a million copies in Canada."

podcast.body: The bulk of this album was written on the stage of Queen's University 25 years before July 2016, highlighting the band's deep roots in Kingston. "25 years ago this July we set up our gear on this very stage and wrote the bulk of our psychedelic and road out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This album was the Tragically Hip's first to reach number one in Canada. The band went to Kingsway Studios in New Orleans in September 1990 armed with about a dozen songs for the record, but continued writing and jamming, ending up with far more material than they could use. The producer, Don Smith, focused on microphone placement and non-stop recording, with an ethos to "just keep playing and playing and playing in the studio and never stop recording." Though a double album was discussed, the final decision was to pare down the selection to an even dozen tracks to avoid the "sophomore curse" following *Up To Here*. The original title concept was "Saskadelvia," but it was deemed "too Canadian" by the US record company, leading to the adoption of "Road Apples," which referred to both a game of road hockey with frozen horse manure and a way to "beat the critics to it" by calling their own album "horse shit." Actual road apples encased in Lucite were sent out for promotion. "We called road hockey road apples because in my parents' generation, they would go out and play road hockey with a piece of frozen horse. And those are road apples."

podcast.body: This album's title refers to "road apples," which is a chunk of horse manure. Historically, a frozen road apple could be used as a substitute for a puck when one was unavailable, highlighting a hockey connection. "The title of their second record, Road Apples. What exactly is a Road Apple? Well it's a chunk of horse poo. And back in the day, a frozen Road Apple made for a decent substitute when a puck couldn't be found."

podcast.body: This album, released in February 1991, successfully maintained and built upon the initial success of "Up To Here." Its performance solidified The Tragically Hip's momentum and further demonstrated the Canadian Generation X's strong demand for domestic music. "when road apples appeared in February 1991, it maintained the momentum and built on the initial record success."
